finding.text: All five asks are met in the worktree (`worktree/tag-notes`, c4c85f11c): `TagRouter.page_for` reads the real tree, notes go through the one `Inbox.note` (Servex/agents/inbox.js:154), tags with no page come back in `unrouted`, and the note links the session plus 1-based sentence numbers with no copied text. `node Servex/ext/refine/test/tag-router.mjs` passes all 5 checks.

The owner's smallest slice was "visible in that page's rail", and that has not been shown yet. The doc says as much (ext/Refine/doc/tag-notes-2026-10-12.md:13). After the Servex restart, one real refine with a screenshot of the `/framework/ext/Refine/` rail would close it.

Only prompts that come through `/api/refine` are routed (Servex/Servex.js:673; called from ext/Refine/Prompt.js and RefineSystem.js). If the VS Code Echo pipeline (Servex/doc/echo.md) refines without that route, tags on typed VS Code prompts never reach a page, so this is worth checking.

`tag_notes` goes back only in the HTTP response (Servex/ext/refine/run.js:61) and is never written to the session's prompts.jsonl. Nothing permanent records which notes a prompt left or which tags had no page, and the "listed" ask would last longer as a logged line.

On Windows, `fs.existsSync` ignores case, so a tag like `core/page` or `Servex` matches a folder and returns a path in the tag's own spelling (TagRouter.js:33). The note still lands in the right file, but `sent[].path` may be a URL with the wrong case. Reading back the real folder name would fix it.

`has_note` (TagRouter.js:56) checks for a substring in any `"note"` line, cleared notes included. So once the owner clears a note, re-running the same prompt never adds it back. That is probably the intended behaviour; it is just not written down.

Each note also wakes the page's coordinator if one exists (inbox.js:164). Refine runs on every prompt, so a module that gets tagged a lot could wake its agent often. Watch the volume once this is live.
The brief said "commit each step", but the work landed as one commit. It is small enough that this does no harm.
